39374.question_text: A patter of beats to denote movement in poetry is
39374.explanation: In poetry, metre refers to the pattern of beats or stresses in a line of verse. This regular rhythm creates a sense of movement and flow, which is why it is described as the “beat” of a poem.

39375.subject: Literature in English
39375.question_text: The extract is an example of a/an
39375.explanation:
An epigram is a brief, witty, and often paradoxical statement. The extract presents a paradox:

  • "Whose word no man relies on" suggests the king was unreliable.

  • "Who never said a foolish thing / And never did a wise one" contrasts his words and actions, implying irony.

This sharp, concise, and witty structure is characteristic of an epigram.

39377.subject: Literature in English
39377.question_text: A poem whose shape resembles the object described is a/an
39377.explanation: An emblematic poem (also called a pattern poem or concrete poem) is a poem arranged on the page so that its shape visually represents the object or idea being described. For example, a poem about a tree may be shaped like a tree on the page.

39451.subject: Literature in English
39451.explanation:
The underlined expression:

“An army forever on the move, forever vigilant: an army without drums, without gleaming uniforms.”

shows parallelism because of the deliberate repetition of similar grammatical structures:

  • “forever on the move, forever vigilant”

  • “without drums, without gleaming uniforms”

This balanced and repeated structure is used to emphasise the teachers’ continuous effort and quiet dedication.

39454.subject: Literature in English
39454.question_text: ''The flag of knowledge and morality'' illustrates
39454.explanation:
The phrase:

“The flag of knowledge and morality”

is a metaphor because it compares knowledge and morality to a flag without using “like” or “as.” The flag symbolises the teacher’s mission and values—their work in spreading knowledge and moral guidance—figuratively representing their ideals.

39485.subject: Literature in English
39485.explanation:
The extract is from William Shakespeare's The Tempest. The speaker is Ceres, a spirit and Roman goddess of agriculture.

  • "Tell me, heavenly bow" → She is addressing Iris, another spirit, who serves the goddess Juno.
  • "If Venus or her son" → Refers to Venus (goddess of love) and Cupid (her son).
  • "Do now attend the queen?" → She is asking whether Venus and Cupid are present.
  • "Since they did plot... my daughter got" → She is upset because Venus and Cupid helped Pluto (Dis) abduct Proserpina (her daughter).
  • "Her and her blind boy’s scandalled company I have forsworn" → She has sworn off Venus and Cupid because of their past actions.

Since Ceres is a goddess (spirit), not a king, sailor, or mortal man, the correct answer is C. Spirit.
